John F. Kennedy could not do one sit-up on the day he became the most powerful man on earth, and the corset his doctors kept him in is why the bullet that killed him found its mark.

He had been in pain since Harvard. In 1954 surgeons bolted a metal plate to his spine. The wound went septic and a priest was called to give him the last rites. A second operation took the plate back out. After that came the anaesthetic needles, sometimes several a day, a rocking chair, crutches kept out of the photographs, and a stiff canvas corset he laced on every morning like a second shirt.

That was the settled treatment for a bad back. Cut it, numb it, strap it up and keep it still.

In October 1961 an Austrian called Hans Kraus was shown into the White House. Kraus was a rock climber who had mended his own fractures by moving them, and he examined the President the way he would a recruit. Kennedy could not sit up from the floor. Asked to touch his toes, he could not reach his knees. The most photographed torso in America had been rested for 20 years and there was very little of it left.

Kraus told him the back was weak, and that weak things are loaded until they are strong. He gave him exercises and then weights, in the little gym beside the White House pool, and said he would walk out if the needles carried on.

It worked almost at once. Within a year Kennedy was picking up his children, which he had not been able to do, and playing golf again. Kraus's notes, handed to the Kennedy Library by his widow in 2006, record a lifelong complaint that was very nearly gone by the autumn of 1963.

The corset was the one thing Kraus could not get off him. He told the President he no longer needed it. Kennedy kept lacing it on.

He was wearing it in the open car in Dallas on 22 November. The first bullet went through the base of his neck. A man with nothing round his middle folds forward at that point, down below the line of the seat. Kennedy stayed bolt upright, held there by canvas and laces, with his head exactly where it had been.

His back was the strongest it had been in 20 years, and he died sitting up straight in the last piece of the old treatment.
